newsitem.title: INDIA: India rescuers sift air crash debris for survivors.
newsitem.headline: India rescuers sift air crash debris for survivors.

text.p: About 350 people were feared killed on Tuesday when a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet taking off from New Delhi and an incoming Kazakh airliner slammed into each other in the world's worst mid-air collision.

Wreckage and burning bodies, some recognisable as women and children, were littered over six kilometres (four miles) of fields near the village of Charkhi Dadri in Haryana State, 80 km (50 miles) southwest of India's capital, New Delhi.
Involved in the collision were a Saudi Arabian Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 cargo aircraft which, officials said, carried between them a total of 350 pasengers and crew.
Senior police official V. B. Singh told Reuters: "Our first priority is to look for survivors, of which there is very little hope."
Rescue workers, battling flames and other hazards, recovered 275 bodies by late Tuesday, the United News of India reported.
They worked in darkness on a moonless night, using hurricane lanterns and torches to light the fields where the flaming debris of the airliners plunged to earth.
Tractors were used to haul away scores of bodies.

The stench of burnt human flesh, mingled with the smell of burning rubber, chemicals and plastic, was heavy over the site, where the silhouette of one airplane with its roof sliced off, was faintly visible.
"We have seen nothing like this before," one of the rescue workers, with a white handkerchief shrouding his face, told Reuters. "It is bizarre and sickening."
A police official said it was thought there were three or four survivors "but they died on the way to hospital in Charkhi Dadri".
Villagers crowded around the crash site and more than 300 police cordoned off the area where the impact of the debris ploughed craters up 10 feet (three metres) deep.
A U.S. Air Force pilot flying nearby reported seeing two fireballs plunge to earth from an altitude of about 15,000 ft (4,570 metres).

"In the distance off our right-hand side, two fireballs seemed to appear... diverging away from each other," the pilot, who was bringing a military cargo plane into New Delhi, told reporters in Washington by telephone.
"The two fireballs proceeded to descend down and hit the ground and became fireballs on the ground," he said.

Officials said there were 312 people, including 23 crew, aboard Saudi Arabian Airlines flight SV 763, a Boeing 747, bound for Dhahran and Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. Most of the passengers were Indians and Nepalese.
Kazakh Airlines flight KZA 1907, an Ilyushin Il-76 cargo plane, had 28 passengers and 10 crew, according to transport officials in the Central Asian state.
It was flying from Chimkent in Kazakhstan to New Delhi. It had been chartered by a company in neighbouring Kyrgyzstan and most of the passengers aboard were Kyrgyz.
PTI said there were 17 foreigners on the 747.
If the toll of 350 is confirmed, the air disaster will be among the world's five worst for loss of life and the worst involving two aircraft in flight.
Ranjan Chatterjee, chairman of Airports Authority of India said: "We have not heard of any survivors so far. It seems rather difficult, unfortunately.
"Coming from that height of 14,000 to 15,000 feet chances of survival do not appear to be very bright."
He said air traffic control equipment had been functioning normally.
Officials of the directorate general of civil aviation said the Saudi airliner had been cleared to climb to 14,000 ft (4,270 metres) by air traffic control in New Delhi.
The Kazakh airliner had been cleared to descend to 15,000 ft, they said.
"Radar blips of both aircraft disappeared at 1840 hours (1310 GMT), 40 nautical miles southwest of Delhi," one official said.
The Indian government ordered an inquiry, headed by a High Court judge, into the collision, aviation officials said.
The previous worst mid-air accident was when a British Trident and a Yugoslav DC9 collided over Zagreb in 1976 with the loss of 176 lives.
